ai-at-work.title: Sola Security launches Lumina to cut enterprise security alert noise with contextual AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Cybersecurity startup Sola Security Ltd. today announced the launch of Lumina, an autonomous risk intelligence platform that applies contextual artificial intelligence across cloud, identity, software
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Sola Security just launched Lumina, an AI platform designed to filter security noise by giving you prioritized alerts instead of dumping raw data on your team. This matters because your security team is drowning in false positives and alert fatigue is a real threat to actual incident response, so smarter prioritization could actually help them focus on real problems. Here's the thing though: every security vendor claims to reduce noise, and the proof is in whether your team actually stops ignoring alerts or just ignores a different dashboard instead.

ai-at-work.title: LaunchDarkly launches runtime control layer for the agentic AI era
ai-at-work.excerpt: LaunchDarkly, a feature control platform that helps developers and software engineers launch and manage products, today announced the launch of AgentControl, a new solution providing real-time managem
ai-at-work.dwp_take: LaunchDarkly rolled out AgentControl, a new tool designed to manage AI agents in production environments with real-time controls, addressing the fact that AI behaves unpredictably compared to traditional code. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because AI agents are increasingly handling actual work tasks, and you need ways to monitor and adjust them without pulling the plug entirely. Here's the thing though: if your biggest concern right now is managing rogue AI agents, you probably haven't solved the human problems of getting people to actually use your new tools in the first place.

ai-at-work.title: Darwinium pushes mobile fraud detection beyond the login moment
ai-at-work.excerpt: Artificial intelligence fraud prevention platform company Darwinium UK Ltd. today released updates to its Android and iOS mobile software development kits, adding continuous in-session detection of re
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Darwinium released updated mobile SDKs that detect fraud beyond just the login screen, catching ongoing threats like remote access scams and account farming schemes. This matters because your users are getting hit with sophisticated mobile attacks that old-school authentication alone won't stop, and you're liable when your apps become a fraud pipeline. The real question is whether your team has capacity to integrate another security layer or if you're already drowning in vendor integrations.

ai-at-work.title: Everpure pitches storage as the last line of cyber defense in the AI era
ai-at-work.excerpt: Everpure Inc. today reinforced its Enterprise Data Cloud vision by defining the storage layer as the last line of defense in modern cyber resilience, an architecture the company argues is essential as
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Everpure is positioning storage infrastructure as the final defensive layer against cyberattacks in an AI-driven threat landscape, arguing that immutable and resilient storage is critical as attacks become faster and more sophisticated. This matters because digital workplace professionals increasingly need to think about data protection holistically rather than relying solely on perimeter defenses, and storage architecture decisions now directly impact business continuity. That said, calling storage "the last line of defense" is a bit like saying your fire extinguisher is your fire prevention strategy, when you really need the whole building designed right in the first place.

industry-news.title: Microsoft refreshes Surface for Business lineup, starts AI PC upsell at $1,499
industry-news.excerpt: Latest hardware adds Intel’s newest AI-focused processors as Redmond continues pushing enterprises toward Copilot+ PCs
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft rolled out refreshed Surface devices packed with Intel's latest AI processors and started pricing the new lineup at $1,499 for businesses looking to upgrade. This matters because IT leaders now face real budget decisions: whether these AI-capable machines justify the premium or whether existing hardware will do the job fine for most users. Here's the thing, though: slapping a neural processing unit on a device doesn't automatically mean your organization needs to drop fifteen hundred bucks per seat unless you've actually got workloads that benefit from on-device AI processing, and most shops don't yet.
